instructions: Open your library (Notion / Obsidian / text file).
Save the adapted prompt with the tag 'adapted: <your context>'.
Bookmark the template in Cmd+K so it's at hand.
After a week — review: what works, what doesn't.
s5.example:
# Prompt library

## /dev-task — for my project

prompting-techniques.title: Prompting techniques: hands-on
prompting-techniques.subtitle: Few-shot, CoT, XML, Prefill, Structured output — on one task
prompting-techniques.whatItIs: A workshop on 5 fundamental techniques that turn an 'average' prompt into a reliable tool. You apply each technique to the same task to see what each one affects.
prompting-techniques.approach: One baseline prompt → 5 versions with different techniques → comparison. Without comparison you won't feel the effect; with it — the techniques settle into muscle memory.
outcomes: Apply Few-shot, CoT, XML, Prefill consciously — to a specific problem
Get JSON output that parses on the first try
Know which technique helps with which prompt failure

applyIn.title: Exact format
applyIn.description: If you need JSON/table/markdown — Prefill + Structured output technique.

applyIn.description: Analytics, cause-and-effect chains — Chain of Thought.

applyIn.title: Subtle style / tone
applyIn.description: Brand voice, a specific report format — Few-shot examples.

pitfalls: Applying all 5 techniques at once — you won't know what helped. Use one at a time.
Giving contradictory few-shot examples — the model will pick a random pattern.
Prefilling a long starting text — the model stretches to reach it and loses quality. 1–3 anchor tokens is enough.
Asking for 'JSON' without a schema and example — Claude will invent the fields.

exercises.question: Take your baseline prompt and make 5 versions: +CoT, +Few-shot, +XML, +Prefill, +Structured. Compare results.
exercises.hint: Works best on a medium-difficulty task — a simple one will be solved by one technique; a very complex one won't be saved by five.

exercises.question: Find a task in your work routine where you currently manually parse Claude's answer. Rewrite the prompt using Structured output.

exercises.hint: After each iteration write down: what improved, what broke.

s1.title: Lock in a baseline prompt
s1.why: Without a baseline you won't see what each technique improved.
instructions: Take a real task from your work (document audit / data analysis / text structuring).
Phrase the prompt in ONE line — the way you'd normally write in a chat. Example: 'Analyze this text and give conclusions.'
Run in Sonnet, save the result as the baseline.
s1.validate: You have a one-liner prompt + Claude's answer as the baseline.
s1.tip: The more 'average' the baseline quality — the more noticeable the technique's effect. A great baseline is already good; a terrible one — techniques won't save it.

s2.title: Apply Chain of Thought
s2.why: CoT (Chain-of-Thought — asking AI to "think out loud" step by step) gives +20–40% accuracy on tasks where you need to 'derive', not 'recall'.
instructions: Add to the baseline: 'Think step by step. First list the facts, then hypotheses, then conclusions.'
Run in a new chat on the same task. Example prompt: 'Analyze this text. Think step by step: 1) list the facts 2) formulate 2–3 hypotheses 3) check each one 4) give a recommendation.'
Compare the reasoning depth with the baseline.
s2.validate: The answer contains explicit reasoning stages, not just the conclusion.
s2.tip: CoT is not needed for simple questions — just a longer answer. Use it where there's 'logic', not 'fact'.

s3.title: Add Few-shot examples
s3.why: Few-shot (a handful of examples in the prompt that AI mimics) is the most powerful technique for non-standard formats and tone.
instructions: Come up with 2 mini-examples: what input → what output you want.

Structure: 'Example 1: input: ... output: ... Example 2: ... Now do for: ...'. Example prompt: 'Example 1: input: <short text> → output: <in your format>. Example 2: input: <another text> → output: <in your format>. Now do for: <your real input>.'
Run. Check — did the model reproduce the style of the examples?

If the model copies the example verbatim — the examples are too close to your input: make them on-topic but not same-content. If it ignores the example format — add explicitly: 'Format — strictly as in the examples'.
s3.validate: Output follows the pattern of the examples, not its 'own'.
s3.tip: 2–3 examples are usually better than 5+ — more noise, not signal. Use varied examples.

s4.title: Structure with XML tags
s4.why: XML gives +2–3× stability on long prompts with different data types.
instructions: Split the prompt into blocks: <context>, <task>, <examples>, <constraints>.

Put each piece in its own tag. Text inside — plain. Example: '<context>...</context> <task>Analyze the text from <input></task> <input>...</input> <constraints>English only. No introductory phrases. Maximum 5 points.</constraints>'
Run. Notice — the model 'confuses' data and instructions less.
s4.validate: The prompt reads as a structure, not a 'wall of text'. The model clearly separates data from instructions.
s4.tip: XML is for long prompts with different blocks. On a short request — overkill.

s5.title: Lock in format via Prefill and get JSON (Structured output)
s5.why: Prefill firmly sets the start of the answer — the model doesn't 'drift' from the format; together with Structured output it turns the answer into parseable JSON.
instructions: Prefill: in the chat write 'Start the answer exactly with <YOUR_ANCHOR>'. Anchor = the first character of the needed format: { for JSON, | for a table, # for a markdown heading. Example: '<your request>. Start the answer exactly with | (this is a markdown table). No preamble.' In the API, prefill goes as a role: 'assistant' message at the end of messages — the model continues from it.
Structured output: describe the JSON schema explicitly (which fields, types, enum values), give a mini-example of valid output, and close with a Prefill on `{`.

Example prompt: 'Return JSON with schema: {"summary": string (≤200), "topics": [{"name": string, "weight": "low"|"med"|"high"}], "actions": string[]} Example: {"summary": "...", "topics": [{"name": "X", "weight": "high"}], "actions": ["..."]} Data: <your input>. Start the answer exactly with {. No markdown wrapper.'
Run through JSON.parse() — should work on the first try. If the model adds ```json — prefill didn't work, strengthen: 'WITHOUT markdown wrapper. Raw JSON only'.
If fields are sometimes missing — add 'all fields are required' to the schema. If fields contain extra noise — show a bad and good example: 'don't do this: ...; do this: ...'.
s5.validate: The answer starts with your anchor, without 'Sure, here is...' openers; JSON parses on the first try, fields match the schema.
s5.tip: Prefill 1–3 anchor tokens — no more. Don't rely on 'the model will figure it out': write the schema and required fields explicitly.

s6.title: Iteration: one failure — one fix
s6.why: A method for improving a prompt without rewriting from scratch.
instructions: Take a prompt that gives ~70%.
Find ONE specific failure (e.g., 'the output is too generic').
Make ONE change (role / constraint / example).
Run on 2–3 different inputs. Record: helped / didn't.
Repeat 2–3 times.
s6.validate: You have v4 vs v1 of the prompt — a noticeable difference without a full rewrite.
s6.tip: Change 5 things at once — you won't know what helped. One step = one hypothesis.

troubleshoot.Agent doesn't start on 'do a security re: Description is too generic or conflicts with another agent. Make it unique.
troubleshoot.Starts on irrelevant requests: Description is too broad. Add negative triggers: 'Use ONLY when ...'.

sa-6.title: Understand the Skill vs Subagent difference
sa-6.why: The final lock-in. Without it the confusion will return in a week.

instructions.0: Take 3 of your recurring tasks.
instructions.1: For each answer: is context isolation needed? Are custom tools needed? Is the task long?
instructions.2: All 'yes' → subagent. All 'no' → Skill. Mixed → think more.
instructions.3: Record the choice in a table: Task → Skill | Subagent | Hybrid.

sa-6.validate: You have 3 tasks with a justified tool choice. You can explain the choice in words.
sa-6.tip: Hybrid is also possible: a Skill invokes a Subagent for the heavy part — best of both worlds.

subagents.trigger: You're confused: how is a Skill different from a Subagent — and when to use which.
outputs: Working subagent with isolated context
Clear separation Skill (how to do) vs Subagent (who does)
Invocation command and result check

tool-use.title: Tool use: give Claude hands
tool-use.subtitle: Function calling — the foundation of integrations, agents and MCP
tool-use.whatItIs: [[node:cap-tools|Tool use]] (function calling) is the mechanism through which Claude calls your functions via a JSON schema. It's the basis of MCP, custom agents, and any integrations. After this workshop you understand the architecture from the inside, not as 'magic'.
tool-use.approach: Without good tool descriptions the agent will constantly make mistakes. First learn to write descriptions, then design tool sets. The actual call code is secondary — the SDK writes it.

outcomes.0: Understand the tool use flow: schema → tool selection → call → result → answer
outcomes.1: Describe a tool so Claude picks the right one 95% of the time
outcomes.2: Know when tool use beats MCP and when it's the reverse
outcomes.3: Competently design a tool set for your agent

0.title: Your own agent
0.description: Any custom agent = a system of tools. Without understanding tool use you can't build an agent.

1.title: Product integration
1.description: Claude in your app calling functions from your backend — that's tool use.

2.title: MCP architecture
2.description: An MCP server = just tools on a standard protocol. Understand tool use, you understand MCP.

pitfalls.0: Providing tools without a clear description of effects — Claude will call a destructive one with the wrong arguments.
pitfalls.1: Making a 'universal' tool with 10 parameters instead of 3 narrow ones — Claude gets confused.
pitfalls.2: Not separating read and write tools — the model mixes queries and changes.
pitfalls.3: Relying on 'the model will figure out' the parameter types — describe JSON Schema strictly.

0.question: Take a task from work (e.g., 'respond to support tickets'). Design 3–5 tools for an agent: names, parameters, effects.
0.hint: Separate read (get_ticket, list_recent) and write (reply, escalate). Each — narrow.

1.question: Take one tool from your project and write 2 versions of the description: bad (1 phrase) and good (what, when, what NOT to do). Compare Claude's choices.
1.hint: Good description = when to apply + when not to apply + example arguments.

2.question: Find a process in your work where you currently use free chat. Design how it would look through tool use.
2.hint: If the task = 'find and do' — that's an ideal tool use candidate.

tu-1.title: Understand tool use in plain terms
tu-1.why: Without an interaction model the next steps are someone else's kitchen.

instructions.0: Read the flow schema: User → Claude → Claude picks a tool → your system executes → result → Claude forms the answer.
instructions.1: Notice: Claude does NOT execute code. It only decides 'which tool to call and with what arguments'.
instructions.2: Execution is on your side (SDK / MCP-server / your backend).

tu-1.validate: You can explain in 30 seconds: who does what in the tool use flow.
tu-1.tip: This is exactly the same pattern as MCP — it's a standardized transport between Claude and tools.

tu-2.title: Read the minimal JSON tool schema
tu-2.why: This is the format Claude sees. Mastering it is mandatory.

instructions.0: Open the example: name + description + input_schema (JSON Schema).
instructions.1: Notice: input_schema describes parameters via type, description, enum, required.
instructions.2: Description is the most important part. Claude reads it to decide 'apply or not'.
instructions.3: Example: name: "get_weather", description: "Get current weather for a city. Use ONLY when user asks about current weather, not forecasts.", input_schema: { city: { type: "string" } }.

tu-2.validate: You can write a schema from scratch for a tool 'send email' — name, description, parameters.
tu-2.tip: Anthropic SDK / MCP / [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — all use the same schema. Learn once — apply everywhere.

tu-3.title: Write a good description
tu-3.why: The most common reason 'the agent doesn't work' — a bad description.

instructions.0: Template: WHAT it does (1 phrase) → WHEN to apply (trigger) → WHEN NOT to apply (anti-trigger) → EXAMPLE arguments.
instructions.1: Take your tool from exercise 2. Write the description using the template.
instructions.2: Test: give 3 different user requests — Claude should correctly decide whether to use the tool.

tu-3.prompt: description: "Send transactional email to a user (e.g. order confirmation, password reset). Use when user explicitly asks to notify a person. Do NOT use for marketing emails — those go through marketing_send. Example args: {to: \"user@x.com\", template: \"order-confirmed\", vars: {order_id: \"42\"}}"
tu-3.validate: Description contains when to apply + anti-trigger + example.
tu-3.tip: One paragraph of description often = the difference between 60% accuracy and 95%. Don't skimp.

tu-4.title: Design a narrow tool set
tu-4.why: Narrow tools = reliable agent. Broad = confusion.

instructions.0: Take the task from exercise 1. Split into read / write tools.
instructions.1: Each tool — one goal, no more than 3–5 parameters.
instructions.2: Dangerous actions (write / delete) — separate tools with an explicit confirm flag.
instructions.3: No more than 10 tools per agent. If more — split into two agents.

tu-4.validate: You have 3–7 tools, each narrow, read and write separated, dangerous ones separate.
tu-4.tip: Good sign: you can say about each tool 'when I would use it'. If you struggle — it's either redundant or poorly described.

troubleshoot.Got 15 tools: Some are redundant. Merge similar ones (if parameters align) or split the agent in two.
troubleshoot.One tool with 8 parameters: Split into 2–3 narrow ones — Claude will choose more precisely.

tu-5.title: Decide: tool use vs MCP
tu-5.why: When to write it yourself, when to use MCP.

instructions.0: Direct tool use = when tools are specific to your product, nobody else needs them.
instructions.1: MCP = when tools can be useful to multiple clients / reusable / standardization is needed.
instructions.2: Compare: is your task reusable? If yes — MCP. If unique — regular tool use.

tu-5.validate: You understand when you build an MCP server, when you just add tools for your own agent.
tu-5.tip: Company-internal CRM = tool use (nobody outside the company uses it). Postgres wrapper = MCP (universally useful).

tu-6.title: Apply to your own task
tu-6.why: Without applying this — it's all theory.

instructions.0: Take one process from work that you repeat >5 times a week.
instructions.1: Describe it as 2–3 tools (or MCP server) on paper / in Notion.
instructions.2: Don't write code — write a spec: name, description, params.

tu-6.validate: You have a specification for a real process. Ready to hand off to a developer / implement yourself.
tu-6.tip: A specification is more valuable than 'I tried to code it' — without one the code will be rewritten 3 times.

tool-use.trigger: You need Claude to call your functions / API — not just produce text.
inputs: Description of the function to call
outputs: Working tool_use loop with JSON schema
Understanding of ToolResult and error handling
Foundation for MCP / agents / integrations
tool-use.savings: ~80% integration time vs hand-parsing text responses

hooks.title: Hooks: automating discipline
hooks.subtitle: Guaranteed actions on events — no more 'I hope it won't forget'
hooks.whatItIs: Hooks are shell commands that [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] executes on events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, etc.). They run AT THE HARNESS LEVEL, not the model level. So they're reliable: the model cannot 'forget' a hook.
hooks.approach: Hooks are code, not text. First understand events and environment variables, then write your first hook on a safe action (file formatting). Only then — on sensitive ones (deny on rm -rf).

outcomes.0: Know all the key events (Pre/Post ToolUse, Stop, UserPromptSubmit)
outcomes.1: Set up 2–3 working hooks: auto-format, guard on dangerous commands, post-edit checks
outcomes.2: Understand the difference: hook vs slash-command vs subagent
outcomes.3: Can share hooks with the team via settings.json in git

0.title: Code quality
0.description: PostToolUse:Write → prettier / linter. Guaranteed format on every edit.

1.title: Security
1.description: PreToolUse:Bash → block dangerous commands (rm -rf, git push --force) before execution.

2.title: Metrics / observability
2.description: Stop → log the session to jsonl. See what Claude did and how many tokens it spent.

pitfalls.0: A heavy shell script in a hook — slows every Claude action. A hook must be fast (<500ms).
pitfalls.1: A hook that edits the same file — can get into an infinite loop with the model. Use PostToolUse:Write carefully.
pitfalls.2: Putting hooks with secrets in the shared settings.json — they end up in git. Sensitive ones go in settings.local.json.
pitfalls.3: Using a hook instead of a subagent for long tasks — a hook blocks. Long tasks → subagent.

0.question: Find a 'after every edit of X — do Y' task in your workflow. Implement it as a PostToolUse hook.
0.hint: Classics: prettier after Write, npm test after Edit on a test file, git status after Bash.

1.question: Find a dangerous command you don't trust Claude with. Make a PreToolUse hook that blocks it.
1.hint: Template: check $CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND via grep -E for the pattern → exit 1 on match.

2.question: Make a Stop hook that logs the session end to .claude/logs/session.jsonl. Use for analytics on 'what I worked on'.

hk-1.title: Understand the event model
hk-1.why: Hooks are tied to events. Know the events — know the possibilities.

instructions.0: Key ones: PreToolUse (before a tool call — can cancel), PostToolUse (after — can react).
instructions.1: Useful: Stop (session end), UserPromptSubmit (new user prompt).
instructions.2: Each event provides environment variables: $CLAUDE_FILE_PATH, $CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND, $CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME.

hk-1.validate: You can name 3 events and for each — a typical use scenario.
hk-1.tip: Pre vs Post — a common source of confusion. Pre = before, you can block. Post = after, you can react.

hk-2.title: Open settings.json and find the hooks section

instructions.0: Open .claude/settings.json in the repo. If it doesn't exist — create it.
instructions.1: Find or add the section: "hooks": { ... }.
instructions.2: Under each event — an array of commands: "PostToolUse:Write": [{"command": "..."}].

hk-2.validate: You have valid JSON with an empty hooks block.
hk-2.tip: Hooks in settings.json go into git. In settings.local.json — local only. Choose consciously.

hk-3.title: Write your first hook — auto-format

instructions.0: Add: "PostToolUse:Write": [{"command": "npx prettier --write $CLAUDE_FILE_PATH 2>/dev/null || true"}].
instructions.1: Restart Claude Code to pick up the settings.
instructions.2: Ask Claude to edit a file. After the Write — you'll see that prettier ran.
instructions.3: || true at the end — so the hook doesn't fail if the file isn't supported by prettier.

hk-3.validate: After any Claude edit — the file is automatically formatted.
hk-3.tip: The same template works for biome, eslint --fix, ruff format — any formatters.

troubleshoot.Hook doesn't fire: Check: did you restart Claude? The filename must match the prettier pattern.
troubleshoot.Claude hangs after Write: The hook is too slow. Add a timeout or move to background.

hk-4.title: Protect yourself from dangerous commands with a PreToolUse hook
hk-4.why: A real guard. Especially important if you've allowed Bash in permissions.

instructions.0: Add: "PreToolUse:Bash": [{"command": "echo \"$CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND\" | grep -qE \"rm -rf|git push --force|git reset --hard\" && exit 1 || exit 0"}].
instructions.1: Restart Claude. Ask Claude to run rm -rf temp/.
instructions.2: The hook should block — Claude gets an error and doesn't run the command.

hk-4.validate: The dangerous command is blocked before execution; a safe command passes.
hk-4.tip: This is deny-by-pattern, complementing permissions.deny. Useful when permissions are too broad.

hk-5.title: Log the session via a Stop hook

instructions.0: Add: "Stop": [{"command": "echo \"$(date +%s),$CLAUDE_SESSION_ID,$CLAUDE_TOTAL_TOKENS\" >> .claude/logs/session.csv"}].
instructions.1: mkdir -p .claude/logs.
instructions.2: Work with Claude. Close the session.
instructions.3: Open .claude/logs/session.csv — your stats are there.

hk-5.validate: Sessions are logged with timestamp + tokens.
hk-5.tip: Over the long run, these stats will show which tasks are expensive and which are cheap. Useful for optimization.

hk-6.title: Decide: hook vs slash vs subagent

instructions.0: Hook — on an event, synchronous, fast (<500ms), no decision logic.
instructions.1: Slash command — on a user trigger, can be long-running.
instructions.2: Subagent — a parallel task with context isolation.
instructions.3: Take 3 of your needs → choose a tool for each.

hk-6.validate: You can justify the choice for 3 tasks — why specifically hook / slash / subagent.
hk-6.tip: Hooks are especially valuable for guaranteed actions — the model might 'forget', a hook won't.

hooks.trigger: Claude Code sometimes "forgets" to run tests/lint before a commit — you need hard discipline.
inputs: List of events to intercept (PreToolUse, Stop, ...)
outputs: Working hooks config in settings.json
Automatic lint/test/format on the right events
Guarantee the model can't "forget"
hooks.savings: ~20-30 min/day on manual checks + zero "forgotten" tests

first-project.title: Create your first project with Claude
first-project.subtitle: From an empty computer to Claude Code running
first-project.whatItIs: An end-to-end tutorial for the absolute beginner: install Node.js, open the terminal, create a folder, install [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]], run the first [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] and send the first real prompt. No assumption that "you already know cd".
first-project.approach: The tutorial branches at step 1: [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] (no terminal, you finish at step 2) or Claude Code (everything through step 6). Pick by what matters: a quick start without installs, or full control over the project files.
outcomes: Understand the difference between a claude.ai Project and a local folder
Installed Node.js and can check the version
Opened the terminal and don't fear it
Created your first working folder (two ways)
Installed Claude Code and completed authentication
Generated [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] and sent your first real prompt

applyIn.title: First day with Claude
applyIn.description: Replaces "I read the docs and nothing works" with "in 30 minutes I'm already doing things".

applyIn.title: Onboarding a coworker
applyIn.description: Share the link — and a colleague reaches the same starting state as you in half an hour.

applyIn.title: Clean install
applyIn.description: Got a new Mac or switched to Windows — run the tutorial and rebuild your work environment.

pitfalls: Skipping step 1 (choosing the path) and rushing into the terminal — only to realize a claude.ai Project would have been enough.
Creating a folder with spaces or non-ASCII in the name — then cd complains and you don't know why.
Installing an old Node.js (<18) — Claude Code will complain "engine not supported".
Skipping /init — Claude re-discovers the project every time.

exercises.question: Walk the tutorial to the end along the path you chose at step 1. Time yourself.
exercises.hint: Path A (claude.ai) — 5–10 min. Path B (Claude Code) — 25–35 min.

exercises.question: After finishing — create a second folder for a second project and verify that Claude Code picks up a different CLAUDE.md correctly.
exercises.hint: This checks you understood isolation: one project = one folder = its own context.

s1.title: Choose your path: claude.ai or Claude Code
s1.why: These are two different ways to work with Claude, both valid. Better to choose now than redo it an hour later.
instructions: claude.ai (path A): browser chat, Projects, Artifacts. No terminal. No install. Enough for most tasks: writing, analysis, discussion.
Claude Code (path B): a CLI tool that works with your local files, uses git and MCP. Needs a terminal and Node.js. For development and automation.
Rule of thumb: if your task is "discuss a document" — path A is enough. If it's "edit code in a repo" — path B.
Pick a path and commit: A → go to step 2 and finish. B → go to step 3 and the rest of the tutorial.
s1.validate: You can explain to yourself in one sentence why you picked this path.
s1.tip: Unsure — start with A. Moving to B later is no harder than now.

s2.title: Path A — create a Project in claude.ai
s2.why: A Project is your persistent workspace in claude.ai with its own instructions and knowledge base. This is the final step of the short path.
instructions: Open claude.ai → sign in (Free is enough to start, Pro is needed for Projects).
In the left sidebar find "Projects" → "+ New project".
Name: what you do + for what (e.g., "Regular report audit").
Description: 1–2 lines — what this project is for and what result you expect.
Upload 1–3 files into Project knowledge (if you have any). That's enough to start.

Done. Open the first chat in the Project and send a real prompt. Example prompt: "Using the uploaded files from Project knowledge, do the first analysis for the input: [URL / document / description]. Format — top-5 observations by priority."
If you want to continue along path B later — go to step 3. The knowledge won't be lost.
If there's no Projects section: it's a Pro feature, the Free plan hides it — either upgrade to Pro or work in regular chats without a Project.
If you don't see "New project": you may have a free Team tier — check your subscription in the top-right.
s2.validate: You have a Project with at least one real chat, and Claude's answer is concrete and references the uploaded files.
s2.tip: If you want to continue along path B later — go to step 3. The knowledge won't be lost.

s3.title: Path B — install Node.js and open the terminal
s3.why: Node.js is required to run npm packages, including Claude Code — without it nothing will install. The terminal is the workspace for Claude Code, and it's worth getting over the fear of it.
instructions: Install Node.js, macOS (recommended): open Terminal.app (Cmd+Space → "Terminal" → Enter) and run `brew install node`. If brew isn't installed — install it first from brew.sh.
Install Node.js, macOS (alternative): download the installer from nodejs.org → run the .pkg → follow the steps.
Install Node.js, Windows: download the installer from nodejs.org → run the .msi → tick "Add to PATH" → restart PowerShell.

Verify Node.js: in the terminal run `node -v`. It should print a version like v20.11.0 or newer (≥ 18). `npm -v` should also work. Version 20 or 22 LTS is optimal; 14 or 16 is old and may have issues.

If `command not found: node` — the terminal doesn't see the install: close and reopen it; on Windows make sure you ticked "Add to PATH". If `command not found: brew (mac)` — open brew.sh, copy the install command, run it in the terminal (≈5 minutes).
Open the terminal, macOS: Cmd+Space → "Terminal" → Enter. A black (or white) window with a cursor opens. Windows: Start menu → "PowerShell" or "Windows Terminal" → Enter.
Figure out where you are: run `pwd` (mac) or `pwd` / `echo %cd%` (Windows) → press Enter. It shows the current folder — usually your home: /Users/name (mac) or C:\Users\name (Windows). That's normal.
s3.validate: `node -v` prints version ≥ 18, `npm -v` works; the terminal is open and `pwd` prints the path to your home folder.
s3.tip: The "black screen" does nothing scary on its own. Only specific commands (rm -rf and similar) are dangerous, and you won't type them in this tutorial.

s4.title: Create a working folder and enter it
s4.why: A folder is the "home" of your project — without one, files pile up wherever. And Claude Code operates in the folder where you launched it: if you're not in the right one, Claude will see the wrong files.
instructions: Decide where all your projects will live. I recommend `~/projects/` in home.

Create the folder: `mkdir -p ~/projects/my-first-claude-project` — creates the folder (and the parent `projects/` if it didn't exist). Alternative via Finder/Explorer: open home → create a `projects` folder → inside it another one `my-first-claude-project`.
Name — ASCII only, no spaces. Use hyphens or underscores instead of spaces.
Verify it was created: `ls ~/projects/` (mac) or `dir %USERPROFILE%\projects\` (Windows) — you'll see `my-first-claude-project` in the list.
Enter the folder: `cd ~/projects/my-first-claude-project`. Check: `pwd` → should print /Users/.../projects/my-first-claude-project.

Check what's inside: `ls` (mac) or `dir` (Windows). The folder is empty — that's normal for a new project. Memorize `cd ~/projects/my-first-claude-project` — you'll use it every time you start working.

If `permission denied` — you're creating a folder where you don't have rights: ~/ (home) is always yours, don't create folders in /Applications or /System. If `mkdir: -p: command not found` — you're on Windows in cmd.exe (old): switch to PowerShell or use `mkdir my-first-claude-project` without `-p`.
s4.validate: The folder exists, `pwd` prints the path to the new folder — you're in it.
s4.tip: `cd ..` — go up one level. `cd ~` — return home. The project name is easy to change later — it's just a folder; the key things are ASCII and no spaces.

s5.title: Install Claude Code and complete authentication
s5.why: Claude Code is Claude's "hands" in your terminal; after install the `claude` command is available everywhere. First launch is short: you authenticate once via the browser, after that Claude Code remembers you.
instructions: Install Claude Code (any folder): `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. Wait 30–60 seconds — npm will download and install the package globally.
Verify the install: `claude --version` → it should print the version number with no errors.

If you get EACCES — on mac/Linux run with sudo: `sudo npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, or configure npm prefix into your own folder (~/.npm-global, google "npm permission EACCES"). If EEXIST — an old version is installed: `npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then install again.
Make sure you're in your working folder: `pwd` → my-first-claude-project. Run: `claude`.
A browser opens with Anthropic auth → sign in with the same account as in claude.ai. Return to the terminal — you'll see Claude Code's interactive prompt, you can type messages.
If the browser doesn't open — copy the URL from the terminal manually and open it in the browser.
s5.validate: `claude --version` works; the terminal shows Claude Code's input field and the session is active.
s5.tip: If you accidentally closed the session — just run `claude` again from the same folder. The session's context isn't preserved, but [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] (if you have one) is picked up on the next launch.

s6.title: Create CLAUDE.md via /init and send your first real prompt
s6.why: CLAUDE.md is the project's "character": Claude reads it on every launch so it doesn't ask the same questions. And without a real prompt all of this is just an exercise — the first prompt is what the whole tutorial was for.
instructions: In the Claude session run: `/init`. Claude scans the folder (it's empty right now — that's fine) and suggests a CLAUDE.md draft.
Read the draft. Remove what doesn't fit. Add rules — e.g., "I'm not a developer, explain in plain words", or "This project is about regular report audits".
Save the file (Ctrl+S or :wq in Vim, depending on your editor). Verify: `ls` (mac) or `dir` (Windows) — you'll see CLAUDE.md in the project folder.
If /init doesn't work — you may have typed it in a regular claude.ai chat, not Claude Code: /init is a Claude Code slash command, make sure you're in the terminal session.
Now think: what real task would you delegate to Claude right now? E.g., "help me structure my notes", "let's analyze this document", "sketch a plan for project X".

Phrase the request in the "Role → Task → Format" style (if you don't remember — do the basics tutorial afterward). Example: "I'm working on <your context>. Help me <specific task> in <markdown / list / table> format. If you need inputs — ask questions."
Send it to Claude Code, read the answer. If Claude wants to create a file — allow it, that's normal in your working folder.
s6.validate: A CLAUDE.md file appeared in the folder with your custom rules; Claude gave a meaningful answer tied to your context, possibly created a file in the project folder.
s6.tip: Don't try to make a perfect CLAUDE.md on the first try — it's a living document. Next learning steps: the basics tutorial — for theory of models and context, the claude-code tutorial — for deeper /security-review, hooks, subagents.

s1.title: pwd — find out where you are now
s1.why: The terminal is always "inside" some folder. Finding out which is the first command of the day.
instructions: Open the terminal (if it isn't already): macOS Cmd+Space → "Terminal"; Windows — PowerShell.
Type: `pwd` (mac/linux/PowerShell) → press Enter.
Look at the output. That's the path to the folder you're in right now.
s1.example:
Mac: /Users/denisa
Windows: C:\Users\denisa
Usually when the terminal starts you're in your home — that's normal.
s1.validate: You see a line like /Users/<name> (mac) or C:\Users\<name> (Windows).
s1.tip: pwd = "print working directory". The simpler the command, the more often you use it. This one — literally every time.

s2.title: ls / dir — look at what's around
s2.why: Without ls you're flying blind. ls shows what folders and files are in the current one.
instructions: macOS / Linux: type `ls` → Enter.
Windows (PowerShell): `ls` works too. Old cmd.exe — `dir`.
Look at the list. That's the contents of your home folder: Documents, Downloads, Desktop, etc.
s2.example:
Mac/Linux output:
Applications  Desktop  Documents  Downloads  Movies  Music  Pictures  projects  Public

Windows output (dir):
  <DIR>  Documents
  <DIR>  Downloads
  ...
s2.validate: You see a list of folders: at least Desktop, Documents, Downloads.
s2.tip: `ls -la` (mac) shows hidden files (starting with .) and details. Useful later when you're looking for the .claude/ folder.

s3.title: mkdir + cd — create a folder and enter it
s3.why: That's the entire "start a new project" toolkit: create a folder → enter it.
instructions: Create a test folder: `mkdir tutorial-sandbox` → Enter.
Check it appeared: `ls` → it should be in the list.
Enter it: `cd tutorial-sandbox` → Enter.
Verify you're inside: `pwd` → should end with /tutorial-sandbox.
s3.validate: pwd prints a path ending with /tutorial-sandbox. Folder created, you're in it.
s3.tip: Tab is your best friend. Start typing `cd tut` → press Tab → the terminal completes to `cd tutorial-sandbox/`. Saves 90% of typing.

s4.title: cd .. and cd ~ — navigate back
s4.why: Knowing how to go back is as important as going in. Insurance against "where did I end up?".
instructions: You're now in tutorial-sandbox. Type `cd ..` → Enter. (Two dots = "folder above".)
Check: `pwd` → you're back in home.
Now go back in: `cd tutorial-sandbox` → verify pwd.
From anywhere you can return home with one command: `cd ~` (or just `cd`).
s4.validate: You understand: `..` = up one level, `~` = home, any path = a specific place.
s4.tip: On Windows the tilde (~) also works in PowerShell. `cd` with no arguments always returns home.

s5.title: Lock it in — a nested structure in one command
s5.why: Real task: create ~/projects/<name>/notes/ in one go. `mkdir -p` can do it.
instructions: From anywhere type: `mkdir -p ~/projects/my-first-project/notes` → Enter.
Enter it: `cd ~/projects/my-first-project` → check `ls` (you should see the notes folder).
You can delete the test: `cd ~` → then `rm -r tutorial-sandbox` (Mac/Linux) or `Remove-Item -Recurse tutorial-sandbox` (PowerShell). This removes the folder permanently.
Don't delete ~/projects/my-first-project — it'll come in handy in the first-project tutorial.
s5.validate: You see the notes folder inside ~/projects/my-first-project. Structure created in one command.
s5.tip: -p (parents) is a super useful flag. Without it, mkdir fails if the parent folder doesn't exist. With it — creates the whole chain.

troubleshoot.rm doesn't work on Windows: Windows uses `del` or `rmdir /s`. PowerShell handles `Remove-Item -Recurse`. When in doubt — delete via Explorer.
troubleshoot.Tab completion doesn't work: Normal for cmd.exe. Switch to PowerShell or Windows Terminal — autocomplete works there.

s6.title: Ctrl+C and clear — safely cancel and tidy up
s6.why: Sooner or later a command will "hang" or you'll change your mind halfway. Knowing how to stop it is peace of mind: you can always hit "cancel" without breaking anything.
instructions: Run an "endless" command so there's something to interrupt: `ping example.com` (Mac/Linux) — lines will scroll forever.
Press `Ctrl+C` — the command stops and you get the prompt back. It's safe: Ctrl+C just interrupts the current command, it doesn't touch your files.
If you've half-typed a line and changed your mind — press `Ctrl+C` again: the terminal clears the line so you can start over.
When the screen is cluttered with output — type `clear` (Mac/Linux/PowerShell) → Enter. The screen clears, but your command history stays (the up arrow brings back past commands).
s6.example:
$ ping example.com
PING example.com ...
64 bytes from ...
^C        ← here you pressed Ctrl+C
$         ← prompt is back, everything under control
s6.validate: After Ctrl+C the command stopped and the prompt ($ or >) returned. After `clear` the screen is clean, and the up arrow still shows past commands.
s6.tip: `Ctrl+C` means "interrupt", not "copy" (a habit from other apps). To confirm a command finished rather than hung — watch the prompt: `$` / `>` is back = the command is done.

troubleshoot.Ctrl+C does nothing: Sometimes you need to press it twice. If it's really stuck — close the terminal tab and open a new one: no files are harmed by this.
troubleshoot.clear made my command history disappear: It didn't. `clear` only wipes the visible screen. Press the up arrow — your past commands are still there.

terminal-tour.trigger: The terminal scares you — but Claude Code won't run without it.
outputs: Mastered cd / ls / mkdir / pwd / clear
Sense of "where am I" in the filesystem
"I'll break the computer" fear removed
terminal-tour.savings: ~hours of googling "how to open a folder in the console"

folders-workshop.title: Folders workshop: 3 structure examples
folders-workshop.subtitle: Audits, notes, experiment — build structure for three real cases
folders-workshop.whatItIs: Want to create folders with clicks in Finder/Explorer, or with a command in the terminal — your choice. This tutorial shows both ways across three live scenarios: work reports, personal notes, a throwaway experiment.
folders-workshop.approach: Don't pick ONE way. Create every folder both ways — via Finder AND via mkdir. After 3 rounds, your preference becomes deliberate.
outcomes: Create folders via both UI and terminal
Know which names won't cause problems
Understand how to organize the project tree meaningfully
Can cleanly delete temporary experiments

applyIn.title: Every new project
applyIn.description: First step — a folder with a meaningful name in ~/projects/. Otherwise — chaos in a month.

applyIn.title: Personal knowledge base
applyIn.description: A separate hierarchy for notes, learning, recipes — kept apart from work folders.

applyIn.title: Experiment / sandbox
applyIn.description: A "trash" folder you're not afraid to delete. Every professional has one.

pitfalls: Spaces and non-ASCII in names — the terminal and git don't like them. "my project" ❌ → "my-project" ✅.
Folders on the Desktop — a week later there are 30 of them and you can't find anything. Use ~/projects/.
Deleting a folder with rm -rf without checking — it's gone forever. ls first, then rm.

exercises.question: Create your own ~/projects/ structure: at least 3 projects with meaningful names. One via Finder, two via mkdir.
exercises.hint: Names should answer "what is this?" 6 months later. "test" — bad. "monthly-reports-2026" — good.

exercises.question: Delete a temp folder both ways: once via the Trash (drag-to-trash), once via rm -r. Notice the difference.
exercises.hint: Trash → recoverable. rm -r → no, gone forever. When in doubt — Trash.

s1.title: Decide on a name and structure (naming rules)
s1.why: A folder name is a future `cd <this name>` command. Long / spaces / non-ASCII — you'll suffer every time.
instructions: Rule 1: ASCII only. No non-Latin letters.
Rule 2: instead of spaces — hyphens (or underscores). work-reports, not work reports.
Rule 3: the name answers "what's inside?" (≤ 30 chars). monthly-audits is better than stuff.
Rule 4: one folder — one topic. Don't dump different things into one.
s1.example:
Good: monthly-audits, claude-notes, sandbox-2026, website-redesign
Bad: "My projects", stuff, test, untitled folder, new folder (1)
s1.validate: You can explain to yourself: "This folder is about X, the name is short and clear."
s1.tip: If you plan to make a git repo from the folder — pick the name now. Renaming later is possible but noisy.

s2.title: Example 1 — Work audits (via the terminal)
s2.why: Scenario: you plan to do regular audits once a month. You need a shared folder for them.
instructions: Open the terminal.
Type: `mkdir -p ~/projects/monthly-audits/2026-may`. This creates both monthly-audits and the May subfolder.
Enter it: `cd ~/projects/monthly-audits/2026-may`.
Verify: `pwd` — ends with /monthly-audits/2026-may. Structure is ready to use.
s2.validate: You see the full path to 2026-may. Folder created, you're in it.
s2.tip: Subfolders by date (2026-may) follow the "new month = new folder" pattern. Scales very robustly.

s3.title: Example 2 — Notes and learning (via Finder/Explorer)
s3.why: Scenario: you're learning something new and want to keep notes. Visual is more convenient — that's fine.
instructions: macOS: open Finder → Cmd+Shift+H (return to home) → find the projects folder (or create it with Cmd+Shift+N).
Inside projects: right click → New Folder → type `learning-notes` → Enter.
Inside learning-notes — create two more: `claude` and `terminal-basics`.
Windows: open Explorer → navigate to C:\Users\<name>\projects → right click → New Folder. Repeat for subfolders.
s3.example:
The Finder structure:
projects/
  learning-notes/
    claude/
    terminal-basics/
s3.validate: In Finder/Explorer you see the tree: projects → learning-notes → claude / terminal-basics.
s3.tip: Terminal and Finder work on the same filesystem. A folder created in one is visible in the other. You can mix them.

s4.title: Example 3 — Temporary experiment (any method)
s4.why: Scenario: you want to experiment with something — you need a single-use folder you won't regret deleting.
instructions: Create it however you like: `mkdir -p ~/projects/sandbox` (terminal) OR via Finder.
Create some folders and files inside — anything. For example: `cd ~/projects/sandbox && touch test.txt && mkdir notes`.
Check the contents: `ls` — should show test.txt and notes.
Remember: this folder is a deletion candidate in step 5.
s4.prompt:
mkdir -p ~/projects/sandbox
cd ~/projects/sandbox
touch test.txt
mkdir notes
ls
s4.validate: In sandbox you see test.txt and notes/. Folder filled and ready for deletion.
s4.tip: touch creates an empty file in a second. Handy for quick tests. Windows equivalent: `New-Item test.txt` or `echo. > test.txt`.

s5.title: Clean deletion — two ways
s5.why: Learning to delete is as important as learning to create. Otherwise folders pile up endlessly.
instructions: Way 1 (safe) — via Finder/Explorer: open ~/projects/, drag sandbox to the Trash. Can be undone if you change your mind.
Way 2 (fast, irreversible) — `rm -rf ~/projects/sandbox` (mac/linux) or `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force ~/projects/sandbox` (PowerShell).
IMPORTANT: rm -rf deletes INSTANTLY, no Trash. Double-check the path before Enter.
Verify it's gone: `ls ~/projects/` — sandbox is no longer in the list.
s5.example:
Before: $ ls ~/projects/
monthly-audits  learning-notes  sandbox  my-first-project

After:
monthly-audits  learning-notes  my-first-project
s5.validate: ~/projects/ no longer contains sandbox. Experiment closed, working folders intact.
s5.tip: Never type rm -rf / or rm -rf ~/ — it deletes EVERYTHING. Always specify a concrete path and read it twice.

troubleshoot.rm: command not found on Windows: Use PowerShell with `Remove-Item -Recurse` or just Explorer + Delete.
troubleshoot.Trash doesn't restore on mac: Cmd+Shift+Delete empties the Trash. If you already emptied — files are lost (only Time Machine can recover, if enabled).

s6.title: Protect an important folder: your first backup with git
s6.why: Work folders (like monthly-audits) hurt to lose. Set up git once and you get version history and a safety net: even if you delete a file by accident, you can bring it back.
instructions: Go into the folder you want to protect: `cd ~/projects/monthly-audits`.
Create a repository: `git init`. This turns on change tracking inside the folder.
Save the first snapshot: `git add .` then `git commit -m "initial backup"`.
Confirm the snapshot is saved: `git log --oneline` — you'll see your "initial backup" commit.
s6.prompt:
cd ~/projects/monthly-audits
git init
git add .
git commit -m "initial backup"
git log --oneline
s6.validate: git log shows the "initial backup" commit. Your folder now has a restore point.
s6.tip: Run a new `git commit` after every meaningful change — it's like "saving the game": you can always return to a working version. If git isn't installed — on mac run `xcode-select --install`.

outputs: 3 real folder structures created
Both GUI and command approaches mastered
A template for your future projects
folders-workshop.savings: ~30 min per new project + order in your files

welcome.title: Getting to know Claude
welcome.subtitle: What Claude is, what modes it has, and how to set it up for yourself
welcome.whatItIs: The very first lesson. Explains what Claude is, how it differs from other assistants, what its working modes are (Chat, Cowork, Code), and how to make it useful for your own tasks.
welcome.approach: Every step has buttons that open the right place for you. You do not need to hunt for things in the menus. Read, click, try.
outcomes: You know what Claude is and who built it
You understand how Haiku, Sonnet and Opus models differ
You can tell Chat, Cowork and Code apart
You picked the version you need: the website, the app, or Code
You know how to tune Claude with Custom Instructions and Projects

applyIn.title: Light tasks
applyIn.description: A letter, a translation, an explanation, a short summary. Chat at claude.ai is enough.

applyIn.title: Long work on one task
applyIn.description: Going through documents, multi-step tasks. Cowork in the desktop app fits.

applyIn.title: Code and files
applyIn.description: Programming, automation. Claude Code in the terminal is what you want.

pitfalls: Sticking to one mode only. Each one has its strengths. Different tools for different jobs.
Not setting Claude up for yourself. Without Custom Instructions it answers generically, with no idea about your context.
Ignoring model trade-offs. Haiku is fast but less accurate. Opus is smart but slow and pricey.

exercises.question: Open claude.ai and ask Claude to list three points that make it different from ChatGPT.
exercises.hint: Compare the answer with what you read in this lesson. It shows you how Claude thinks about itself.

s1.title: What Claude is
s1.why: To know who you are about to use.
instructions: Claude is a family of smart assistants that reply to you in text. They are built by a company called Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers.
Inside Claude there are three models of different power. Haiku is the fast and cheap one. Sonnet is the middle ground and the default. Opus is the smartest, for hard tasks.
You usually do not pick the model by hand. Claude picks the right one for the task. You can switch in settings when you need to.
Claude looks similar to ChatGPT in spirit, but differs in details. It has longer memory inside one chat, is more careful with facts, and stays calmer on touchy topics.
s1.validate: You understand that Claude is built by Anthropic and comes in three models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus).
s1.tip: Sonnet covers about 95 percent of tasks. Switch to Opus only when you need deeper reasoning.

s2.title: Three ways to work with Claude
s2.why: Understand the difference between modes so you can pick yours.
instructions: Chat. A regular conversation in your browser or app. Ask a question, get an answer. Best for short tasks: letters, translations, explanations, idea brainstorming.

Cowork. A mode in the desktop app where Claude can work with your files, documents and even your screen, step by step. Best for long tasks: working through documents, writing long texts, doing analysis.
Code. A separate tool for programmers. It runs in the terminal on your computer. It can read and change code files, run commands. You only need it if you write code.
Next, we will walk through the modes: we start with the simplest one, Chat, then cover Cowork and Code together. If you are not a programmer, the Code part is safe to skip.
s2.validate: You remember the three names and what they are for: Chat for short tasks, Cowork for long ones, Code for programmers.
s2.tip: Most people only need Chat. Cowork and Code are for those who want to go deeper.

s3.title: Chat. The easiest way to start
s3.why: This is the basic mode everyone starts with. Nothing to install.
instructions: Press the button below to open claude.ai in a new tab.
Sign in by email or through Google. Sign-up is free. You do not need a paid plan to begin.
After signing in you will see an input field. That is Chat.
Copy the question below and paste it into the field. Press send and read the answer.
s3.prompt: In three simple sentences, tell me how you are different from ChatGPT and what you do best.
s3.validate: You got a reply from Claude in Chat on [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]].
s3.tip: If the answer is too long, write: shorter, one sentence. Claude will get it.

s4.title: Cowork and Code. When the task is bigger than one question
s4.why: Cowork is for working on one topic for a while (a long text, going through a document, a report). Code is Claude's most powerful mode for people who work with code. If you are not a programmer, you can just read about Code.
instructions: Cowork lives in a separate app for Mac or Windows. Download it from Claude's website with the button below.

In Cowork you can give Claude files (documents, spreadsheets, images) or grant it screen access. It then works with them on its own, step by step. Examples: go through these 50 pages and surface the key risks; read my email and draft replies; help me write a long article from this outline.
Cowork is not for every task. If you only have a quick question, stay in Chat. Serious Cowork work needs a Pro subscription, but you can try it for free in a limited way.

Claude Code is a tool for developers that runs in your terminal (the dark window with a command line on your computer). It can read and edit code files directly on your disk, run commands, find bugs, refactor, explain unfamiliar code.

Installing Code is one terminal command. It needs Node.js, a free program that runs commands. There is a dedicated tutorial that walks through it. Code does not replace Chat or Cowork, it adds to them. If you are not a programmer, you can skip Code entirely, and that is fine.
s4.validate: You understand that Cowork is the desktop app for long tasks involving files, and Code is a terminal tool for people who work with code.
s4.tip: Not sure whether you need Cowork or Code? Start with Chat. You can always come back to the advanced modes.

actions.label: Install Claude Code step by step

s5.title: Tuning. Make Claude yours
s5.why: By default Claude answers in a generic way. [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] help it understand your context, and Projects are handy when you have a series of similar tasks.
instructions: Custom Instructions is a short message Claude sees inside every conversation of yours. You write your role, your industry, the tone you want, and what NOT to do. Example: I am an accountant in a small business. Answer briefly, without fluff, in simple words. Do not give legal advice.

Where to find it on the website: in claude.ai open your profile (top right), then Settings → Custom Instructions. The desktop app has a similar setting. Set it once and it always works. Update it when something starts to annoy you in the replies.

A Project is a folder where you keep several chats on one topic. All chats inside a Project share knowledge and instructions. Example: a Project called Marketing for company X, with 20 chats all sharing the same uploaded files: the brand guide, past reports, the yearly plan.
Where to find Projects: on claude.ai look in the left menu for Projects, then New Project. Serious use needs a Pro plan. Do not make a Project for a single task, use it for things that repeat.
s5.validate: You understand that Custom Instructions is your profile card for Claude, and a Project is a workspace for a series of related tasks.
s5.tip: Do not write a wall of text in Custom Instructions. Five to ten lines about you and how you want to talk is more than enough.

s6.title: What to do right now
s6.why: Knowledge fades without action. Make at least one move.
instructions: If you are just meeting Claude for the first time, open claude.ai and ask your first question in Chat.
If you already like Claude and want to use it regularly, set up Custom Instructions. The quality jump is large.
If you need long work with files and documents, download the Claude app with Cowork support.
If you are a programmer and want the advanced mode, take the tutorial that installs Claude Code.
s6.validate: You picked what to try next and made at least one click in that direction.
s6.tip: Do not try to master everything in a day. Come back to the map when questions show up in your real work.

welcome.trigger: First touch with Claude — you need a 5-minute map of "what's here and how to use it".
outputs: Clear sense of modes: Chat / Cowork / Code
Realistic expectations from Claude
Pick the first entry point

claude-cowork.title: Your first task with Claude Cowork
claude-cowork.subtitle: From open to result — autonomous workflow
claude-cowork.whatItIs: A hands-on walkthrough of Claude Cowork: open the Desktop app, connect a folder, describe a task as an outcome, let Claude run it, and review the results. You will complete a real file task from start to finish.
claude-cowork.approach: Describe WHAT you want, not HOW to do it. Claude figures out the steps. Start with a small, low-risk task on a test folder — not your critical files. Keep the Desktop app open the entire time.

outcomes.0: Opened Cowork and understand the interface
outcomes.1: Connected a specific folder (not your whole drive)
outcomes.3: Reviewed Claude's plan before approving it
outcomes.4: Checked the finished output and know how to iterate
outcomes.5: Put a proven task on a Scheduled cadence

0.title: File organization
0.description: Sort downloads, rename files by date, group by project — set it up once, run it weekly.

1.title: Document processing
1.description: Extract data from PDFs, summarize meeting notes, convert formats across a folder of files.

2.title: Scheduled automation
2.description: After mastering a task manually, use /schedule to run it automatically on a cadence.

pitfalls.0: Closing the Desktop app mid-task — Cowork stops immediately.
pitfalls.1: Describing HOW to do the task step-by-step — describe the outcome instead.
pitfalls.2: Connecting your entire drive — connect only the specific folder you need.
pitfalls.3: Using Cowork for simple questions — it consumes significantly more usage quota than regular chat.

exercises.question: Run a second Cowork task: ask Claude to create a summary report of all .txt files in your test folder. Review the output and try one correction via natural language.
exercises.hint: Say what is wrong with the result, not how to fix it. Claude will figure out the correction.

exercises.question: Put your file-organization task on a Scheduled cadence (for example, every Monday morning) and on the next run confirm the result arrived without you doing anything.
exercises.hint: The task must run manually at least once first — Scheduled repeats a proven result, it does not debug a new one.

s1.title: Open Cowork in Claude Desktop
s1.why: Cowork only exists in the Desktop app (Mac/Windows). The web version does not have it. You need a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan.

instructions.0: Download and install Claude Desktop from claude.ai/download if you haven't already.
instructions.1: Sign in with your Claude account (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise required).
instructions.2: In the Claude Desktop window, look for the 'Cowork' tab or button — it is separate from the regular chat.
instructions.3: Click it to open the Cowork interface. You will see a task input area and a section for connected folders.

s1.validate: You see the Cowork task interface — different from the regular chat.
s1.tip: Keep the Desktop app open during the entire tutorial. Cowork tasks stop the moment you close the app.

s2.title: Connect a folder
s2.why: Claude needs explicit permission to read and write files. You choose exactly which folder to expose — Claude cannot access anything outside it.

instructions.0: In the Cowork interface, find the 'Connect folder' or 'Add folder' option.
instructions.1: Choose a specific working folder — for example, a 'Cowork-test' folder on your Desktop.
instructions.2: Do NOT connect your entire Documents or Desktop root — start small and specific.
instructions.3: Confirm the connection. The folder should now appear as available in the Cowork context.

s2.validate: Your chosen folder appears as connected. Claude now has read/write access to it.
s2.tip: For your first task, create a test folder with a few non-critical files. This lets you experiment safely.

troubleshoot.Cannot find 'Connect folder' button: Check that you are in the Cowork tab, not the regular chat. The interface is different.
troubleshoot.Permission denied by OS: On macOS, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files & Folders and grant Claude Desktop access.

s3.title: Describe your task as an outcome
s3.why: The key difference from regular chat: describe WHAT you want as a finished result, not the steps to get there. Claude plans the steps itself.

instructions.0: In the Cowork task field, type your task as an outcome.
instructions.1: Be specific: mention the folder, the type of files, and the desired end state.
instructions.2: Include the output format if it matters (e.g. 'create a summary as a .txt file').
instructions.3: Submit the task. Claude will show you a plan BEFORE starting.

s3.example:
Good: 'In the Cowork-test folder, group all files by extension into subfolders (e.g. /images, /docs, /other), then create a file called index.txt that lists what was moved and where.'

Bad: 'First check the folder, then create subfolders, then move each file...' — don't prescribe steps.
s3.validate: Claude presents a plan showing what it will do. Read it before approving.
s3.tip: If the plan looks wrong, type a correction before approving. It is faster to fix the plan than fix the output.

s4.title: Approve and monitor
s4.why: Cowork runs autonomously once approved. You can watch its progress or step away — both are valid. The key is keeping the Desktop app open.

instructions.0: Review Claude's plan carefully — check that it describes what you actually want.
instructions.1: Click Approve (or equivalent) to start the task.
instructions.2: Watch the progress indicator. Claude shows what it is doing at each step.
instructions.3: You can step away — Claude will continue. Come back when it signals completion.
instructions.4: Do not close the Desktop app. If you need to lock your screen, that is fine — just do not quit the application.

s4.validate: Task reaches 100% and Claude shows a summary of what was done.

troubleshoot.Task stopped unexpectedly: Most likely the Desktop app was closed or lost internet. Reopen it and check if the task can be resumed.
troubleshoot.Claude asks for permission mid-task: Some actions (like deletion) require your explicit approval. Read the request and approve or deny.

s5.title: Review the output and iterate
s5.why: Diligence: the first result is a strong draft, not necessarily final. Open the folder, check the files, and correct anything that missed the mark — in natural language.

instructions.0: Open the connected folder in your file manager and check the output.
instructions.1: Compare what Claude did against your original description.
instructions.2: If something is wrong, describe the issue in plain language in the Cowork task field.
instructions.3: For recurring tasks you are satisfied with, type /schedule to set up automatic runs.

s5.validate: Output matches your intent. You know how to describe corrections.
s5.tip: Say what is wrong ('the images folder is missing PDF files that have images embedded'), not how to fix it. Claude will figure out the correction.

s6.title: Put the task on a Scheduled cadence
s6.why: Once a task is proven and the result satisfies you, there is no point running it by hand every time. A Scheduled cadence repeats the already-verified task automatically — for example, every Monday morning — without you lifting a finger.

instructions.0: Make sure the task has already run manually at least once and the result is correct.
instructions.1: In the Cowork task field, type /schedule (or open the Scheduled menu).
instructions.2: Set the cadence in plain words: 'every Monday at 9 AM' or 'once a day'.
instructions.3: Save the schedule and confirm the task appears in the Scheduled list with its next run time.
instructions.4: Remember: the Desktop app must be open at the scheduled run time — otherwise the task will not start.

s6.validate: The task appears in the Scheduled list with a next run time and repeats without your involvement.
s6.tip: Only schedule proven, low-risk tasks. An automatic run repeats the result literally — it will not stop to ask if something in the folder has changed.

ai-limitations.title: Claude's capabilities and limits
ai-limitations.subtitle: What Claude knows, what it doesn't, and how to work with both
ai-limitations.whatItIs: A practical guide to Claude's real boundaries. You will learn why Claude sometimes says wrong things confidently, what it literally cannot do, how the [[node:b-context|context window]] affects long sessions, and — most importantly — strategies that turn limitations into non-issues.
ai-limitations.approach: Do not skip this tutorial thinking limitations are someone else's problem. Every user eventually hits them. The goal is not to avoid Claude but to use it in ways that make its limits irrelevant.
outcomes: Understand what a knowledge cutoff means and when it matters
Recognize hallucinations before they cause problems
Know what Claude structurally cannot do (and what it can with tools)
Understand why long chats degrade in quality
Have 5 concrete strategies to work around limitations
Can quickly verify Claude's facts and citations against primary sources

applyIn.title: Fact-sensitive work

exercises.question: Ask Claude: 'What happened in the news this week?' Then ask: 'What is your training knowledge cutoff?' Compare the two answers. What does this tell you about when to use web search?
exercises.hint: Notice if Claude attempts an answer to the first question or declines. Either response tells you something about how to prompt it correctly.

exercises.question: Ask Claude a question on a niche topic you know well. Deliberately look for one plausible-sounding detail that might be wrong. Can you spot it?
