Documented and ready to share templates with your team

applyIn.title: Marketing and communications
applyIn.description: A content machine with a consistent brand voice: long-form articles, SEO content, email campaigns and posts for multiple channels — Claude adapts one piece of content to all formats.

applyIn.title: Sales and Customer Success
applyIn.description: Personalised outreach, negotiation prep, objection analysis, response templates — Claude helps scale quality without losing personalisation.

applyIn.title: HR and operations management
applyIn.description: From writing JDs to onboarding packages and policies: Claude cuts time spent on administrative documents and helps maintain a consistent tone and standards.

pitfalls: Using one universal prompt for all tasks in the role — every scenario requires its own context and format. Create a separate template for each repeating task.
Publishing Claude-generated content without checking for brand alignment and factual accuracy — especially critical for external communications in sales and marketing.
Ignoring data confidentiality when working with customer or candidate information — use anonymised descriptions and do not input personal data unnecessarily.

exercises.question: Choose the three most time-consuming tasks in your role. Write a prompt for each and test it on a real example. Which of the three gave the best result on the first attempt?
exercises.hint: Tasks with a clear template and standard output format work best with Claude on the first try. Tasks requiring nuance and context improve after a few iterations.

exercises.question: Find a colleague from a different function (Marketing → Sales, HR → Product) and show them your best prompt. Ask them to adapt it to their role. What changed? What stayed the same?
exercises.hint: Prompt structure is usually transferable. Role context and output format change. This will show you what is the essence of the prompt and what is the role-specific layer.

ruc-1.title: Marketing: a content machine with a consistent voice
ruc-1.why: Marketing produces more content than any other function — but every piece must sound the same. Claude solves both challenges simultaneously.
instructions: Brand voice in the [[node:b-system|system prompt]]: add a brand voice description to the [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] — 3–5 adjectives, examples of sentences that sound 'right' and examples that sound 'wrong'. Claude will apply this automatically.

Long-form and SEO: a prompt for an article = topic + target audience + the main question the reader has + keywords + desired length + structure (H2/H3). Ask Claude to write the outline first and approve it before generating the full text.
Email campaigns: use one message as the base — ask Claude to create 3–5 variations of different length and tone (formal / conversational / urgent). A/B testing will show what works best.

Channel adaptation: one piece of content → five formats. Prompt: 'Here is the long-form text: [TEXT]. Adapt it for: (1) LinkedIn post 150 words, (2) Twitter/X thread of 5 tweets, (3) email subject line + preview text, (4) short summary for a newsletter, (5) script for a 60-second video'.
Typical marketer mistake: asking Claude to 'write content' without audience context. Always specify: who the reader is, what they already know, and how they should feel after reading.
ruc-1.tip: Create one reference piece in the Project that perfectly reflects the brand voice. Use it as a reference: 'Write in the same style as this example: [reference]'.
ruc-1.validate: You have created at least one prompt for a specific marketing task and received a result that can be used as a draft without major edits.

ruc-2.title: Sales: from lead to deal
ruc-2.why: Sales requires personalisation at scale — every message must feel hand-crafted, but doing it manually for 50 leads is impossible.
instructions: Personalised outreach: prompt = company profile (industry, size, recent events) + contact profile (role, pain points of the role) + your product + goal of the message (first contact / follow-up / re-engagement). Result: a draft message that only needs to be checked and personalised in 2–3 places.

Objection analysis: create an 'Objection Analysis' skill. Input: the customer's objection as stated. Output: (1) the real concern behind the objection, (2) 2–3 ways to respond, (3) a question that helps understand the depth of the issue.

Negotiation prep: prompt = company name + known deal information + your position + meeting goal. Ask Claude for: likely questions the customer will ask, likely objections, key arguments for your position, red lines that must not be crossed.

After the meeting: 'Here are my notes from the meeting: [NOTES]. Write a follow-up email with: (1) a thank-you, (2) a brief summary of agreements, (3) next steps with deadlines, (4) an open question to keep the dialogue going'.
Important: always verify factual data about the company and customer that Claude includes in messages — hallucinations in sales are especially dangerous.
ruc-2.tip: The best use of Claude in sales is not replacing personalisation but accelerating it. A draft in 30 seconds, personalisation in 2 minutes — instead of writing from scratch in 15 minutes.
ruc-2.validate: You have a template prompt for outreach that you have tested on 3 real leads and received drafts requiring minimal editing.

ruc-3.title: HR: from JD to onboarding
ruc-3.why: HR creates a large volume of repeating documents — and often spends time on them that could be spent working with people.
instructions: Job Descriptions: prompt = role title + key responsibilities (5–7 items) + must-have requirements + nice-to-have + team context + company format. Ask Claude to write a JD that: (1) sounds attractive to the target audience, (2) uses inclusive language, (3) avoids excessive requirements that exclude good candidates.

Structured interviews: 'I am hiring for [ROLE]. Here are 3 key competencies: [LIST]. For each competency create 2 behavioural questions (STAR format) and scoring criteria: excellent / good / insufficient'.

Welcome package for new employees: use a template prompt with variables — employee name, role, team, start date, manager. Claude generates a personalised welcome letter and first-week checklist in 2 minutes.

Policies and guidelines: 'Here is our existing [TOPIC] policy written 3 years ago: [TEXT]. Update it to current standards, make the language clearer, keep the substance. Mark where you made significant changes'.
Confidentiality: never input real candidate or employee names into Claude without their consent. Use initials or role descriptions instead of personal data.
ruc-3.tip: Create a library of template prompts for each HR document type in the Claude Project. One setup session saves several hours every week.
ruc-3.validate: You have written a JD or interview questions with Claude and compared the result to a previous version written manually. Which took less time and was the quality comparable?

ruc-4.title: Product: from Discovery to Spec
ruc-4.why: A Product Manager spends up to 40% of their time writing documents — PRDs, user stories, roadmap justifications. Claude does not replace product thinking but dramatically accelerates turning it into documents.
instructions: User Stories: 'Here are raw notes from user interviews: [NOTES]. Extract 5–7 user stories in the format: As a [role], I want to [action] so that [outcome]. For each add acceptance criteria and a priority (High/Medium/Low) with justification'.

Interview synthesis: 'Here are transcripts from 5 user interviews: [TRANSCRIPTS]. Extract: (1) recurring pain points (with mention frequency), (2) unexpected insights, (3) contradictions across interviews, (4) open questions requiring further research'.

PRD first draft: create a 'First PRD Draft' skill. Input: problem + target audience + proposed solution + constraints. Output: a PRD structure with completed sections and explicit placeholders where data that Claude does not have is needed.

Roadmap justification: 'I am proposing to prioritise [FEATURE] next quarter. Here is the context: [DATA]. Help write a justification for stakeholders including: business case, alternatives we considered, risks and how we mitigate them, success metrics'.
Important: PRD and roadmap contain strategic decisions that you make, not Claude. Use Claude for structure and wording — not for making product decisions.
ruc-4.tip: The best PRD workflow: first describe the problem to Claude in your own words in 5 sentences. Ask it to ask clarifying questions. Answer them. Only then ask for the document draft.
ruc-4.validate: You have used Claude to synthesise real data (interviews or notes) and received structured output that became the basis for a product decision or document.

ruc-5.title: Customer Success: scale without losing quality
ruc-5.why: A CS specialist handles many customers simultaneously — response quality inevitably drops under load. Claude helps maintain a high level at greater volume.
instructions: Response templates with personalisation: create a library of templates for the top 10 request types. Each template is a prompt with variables: customer name, product, issue summary, account context. Claude generates a personalised response based on the template in seconds.

Escalation: 'Here is the correspondence thread with the customer: [HISTORY]. The customer is expressing [DISSATISFACTION LEVEL]. Write: (1) a brief summary of the situation for the manager, (2) the proposed solution with justification, (3) a draft response to the customer'.

Health Score Analysis: 'Here is product usage data for the customer over the last 90 days: [DATA]. What patterns indicate churn risk? Which indicate expansion potential? Suggest 3 specific action items for the CS manager'.

QBR preparation: 'Here is the account data for the quarter: [DATA]. Help prepare a QBR: (1) key achievements that matter specifically to this customer, (2) ROI visualisation, (3) recommendations for the next quarter, (4) open questions for discussion'.

Boundary of application: Claude does not see the relationship history with the customer that you have built. Always provide factual details (figures, agreements, names) explicitly — never assume Claude 'knows' the customer.
ruc-5.tip: The fastest win for CS: create a template for the most frequent request type. The first hour of setup pays off in the first week.
ruc-5.validate: You have a ready response template for at least one request type that you have tested on real cases and it requires minimal editing before sending.

ruc-6.title: Build your role playbook
ruc-6.why: Scattered prompts living in notes do not produce a systemic effect. A playbook turns them into a standard — your personal one or your team's.
instructions: Role playbook structure: (1) Top 5 role tasks with prompts, (2) Recommended Project structure (instructions + knowledge base), (3) Common mistakes to avoid, (4) How to assess output quality, (5) What to never delegate to Claude.
Choose your top 5 scenarios: list five tasks you do every week. For each write a prompt, add an example input and expected output. This is the core of the playbook.
Document anti-patterns: record 2–3 cases where Claude gave a bad result and why. This is the most valuable part of the playbook for colleagues — they learn from your mistakes, not their own.
Format for sharing: a Claude Project with instructions is ideal for storing a playbook. Share access with the team — or export as a Notion/Confluence page with prompts ready to copy.
Living document: add a 'last updated' date and a 15-minute retrospective once a month. Claude and its capabilities change — the playbook must change with them.
ruc-6.tip: The best playbook is minimal but used. Five well-described scenarios beat twenty formal ones. Start small and add as you use it in real work.
ruc-6.validate: You have a role playbook with at least three documented scenarios that you are ready to send to a colleague today. Check: could they use it without your explanations?

inputs: Your function and top 5 weekly tasks
outputs: Role playbook: 5 tasks × ready prompt + Project
Integration map (MCP / KB / templates)
Onboarding plan for peers in the same role

mcp-advanced.title: Advanced MCP: build your own server
mcp-advanced.subtitle: From ready integrations to a production-grade server you own
mcp-advanced.whatItIs:
Off-the-shelf [[node:mcp|MCP]] servers cover 80% of cases. But sooner or later you hit it: an internal service, a legacy DB with a custom schema, a gated API, non-standard auth — no server exists. So you write your own.

Your own MCP is not "hello world in 50 lines". It is a backend component living next to production: transport, schemas, errors, retries, observability, security. This workflow is how to build it so it is not embarrassing in a registry and does not page you at 3 AM.
mcp-advanced.approach: First take the gateway decision (existing vs your own), then a minimal server on the SDK, then layer in resources/prompts, HTTP transport, Inspector, security, publish. Do not write everything at once — grow in layers, each step validated in Inspector.
outcomes: You understand when MCP is the right answer and when it is not
You built a working server on the official TypeScript or Python SDK
You distinguish tools / resources / prompts and know where each belongs
You run stdio and HTTP/SSE transports and understand the trade-off
You debug through MCP Inspector, not through console.log
You closed the security checklist: scopes, sandboxing, secrets, rate limits
You published the server to a registry or internal NPM/PyPI

applyIn.title: Internal data sources
applyIn.description: Your DB, internal REST, gRPC service — expose to Claude without a public API.

applyIn.title: Domain tooling
applyIn.description: Team-custom tools: code search, build system, deploy pipeline.

applyIn.title: Compliance scenarios
applyIn.description: Data cannot leave for SaaS — sandbox server locally, audit log every call.

pitfalls: Writing your own server before understanding the spec — you rewrite it later.
Putting everything in tools — resources and prompts exist for a reason.
Choosing HTTP transport when stdio is enough — auth, TLS, deploy for zero gain.
Ignoring Inspector — debugging through a client is 10× slower.
Exposing tools with broad scopes ("delete_all") without a confirm flow.

exercises.question: Take an internal team API and wrap it in an MCP server with 2 tools and 1 resource. Drive it through Inspector until green.
exercises.hint: Start with read-only tools. Add write operations as a separate step — easier to review.

exercises.question: Compare stdio and HTTP transport for your server. Measure latency, deploy convenience, auth complexity. Make a decision and record the reasoning.
exercises.hint: stdio = local, zero-config, no auth. HTTP = remote, multi-tenant, needs auth. Not "better", different niches.

s1.title: Gateway decision: build your own or take an existing one
s1.why: Your own server is maintenance forever. Verify nothing existing fits before you commit.
instructions: Open the Anthropic MCP registry and the community list (awesome-mcp-servers).
Search by service name plus 2-3 synonyms. Servers are often named non-obviously.
If found — check last commit, open issues, scope. Forking an existing one beats writing from scratch.
If an existing server is missing one operation — open a PR, do not fork. Saves you a year of maintenance.
If nothing fits — write down the 3-5 operations you actually need (not "all of the API").

Example. Internal trace-storage: nothing exists (checked awesome-mcp-servers, npm, PyPI); needed search_traces, get_trace, get_service_map; NOT needed delete and admin operations. Decision: build my own, scope read-only, 3 tools.
Not sure what the spec covers? Open modelcontextprotocol.io/specification — Server features section. Map your list: what is a tool, what is a resource, what is a prompt.
s1.validate: There is a written list of 3-5 operations and a rationale for why existing servers do not fit.
s1.tip: If an existing server is missing one operation — open a PR, do not fork. Saves you a year of maintenance.

s2.title: Minimal server on the SDK + distributing tools/resources/prompts
s2.why: The official SDK handles transport, JSON-RPC, lifecycle — a hand-rolled protocol on sockets is a month of work and bugs. And the spec gives three primitives for a reason: stuff everything into tools and the client cannot cache or surface things to the user properly.
instructions: Pick a language: TypeScript (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) or Python (`mcp`). Use the one you already have infra for.
Scaffold: `npm init mcp-server` or clone the official quickstart template.
Declare ONE tool with a minimal schema and a stub response. No business logic yet.
Run via stdio (`node dist/index.js`), confirm the process stays up.

Distribute the primitives. Tools = actions with side-effects or computation (search, create, calculate) — the model calls them as needed. Resources = data readable by URI (files, DB records, documents) — the client can pre-fetch and show to the user. Prompts = workflow templates the user explicitly picks ("do a code review"), parameterized.

Walk through your list: each operation lands in one of the three. In doubt — tool (most compatible, supported by all clients). Resource vs tool: "would the client want to show this object BEFORE the model mentions it?" If yes — resource.

Distribution example for trace-storage: search_traces → tool (has parameters, computation); get_trace(id) → resource (`trace://abc123`) — client caches; review_incident → prompt (template: "analyze trace X vs baseline Y").

If `TypeError: Cannot find module @modelcontextprotocol/sdk` — run `npm i @modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, make sure package.json has `"type": "module"`. If the process exits immediately — you forgot `await server.connect(transport)`: without `await` the process closes before connection.
s2.validate: Server starts, does not crash, responds to `tools/list`; each operation is mapped to one of three primitives with a written rationale.
s2.tip: In doubt about a primitive — tool. Most compatible primitive, supported by all clients.

s3.title: Debug through MCP Inspector
s3.why: Inspector is the official MCP devtools. Shows JSON-RPC traffic, schema validation, responses. Without it debugging is `console.log` in the dark.
instructions: Launch Inspector: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node dist/index.js`.
A web UI opens on localhost. You see capabilities, tools, resources.
Call each tool with test parameters from the UI. Look at request/response JSON.
Test edge cases: empty params, wrong type, missing required.
Capture found bugs — fix before the next step.
Inspector can also inspect HTTP servers: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --transport http http://localhost:3000`. Useful before deploy.

If Inspector does not connect — check the server writes to stderr, not stdout (stdout is reserved for JSON-RPC). If a tool responds but Inspector shows a schema error — your response does not match the declared outputSchema: either align the response or drop outputSchema (it is optional).
s3.validate: All declared tools/resources are callable through Inspector with correct responses.
s3.tip: Inspector can also inspect HTTP servers: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --transport http http://localhost:3000`. Useful before deploy.

s4.title: HTTP/SSE transport — when and how
s4.why: stdio is great for local dev and Claude Desktop. For a shared team server or remote deploy you need HTTP with SSE for streaming.
instructions: Decide: HTTP is justified if the server is shared (multiple clients) or hosted remotely.
Use `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` from the SDK — it handles SSE.
Add auth middleware: bearer token in header, OAuth, mTLS — pick per security model.
A `/health` endpoint separate from the MCP route — needed for load balancers.
Log a request-id with each response for tracing.

If the SSE connection drops after 30 sec — a proxy (nginx/cloudflare) closes idle: set `proxy_read_timeout 3600s` or enable keep-alive ping in the SDK. CORS errors from a browser client — add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for known origins; do NOT set `*` in prod — leak vulnerability.
s4.validate: Server returns 401 without a token, 200 with a valid one; Inspector connects over HTTP and sees all tools.
s4.tip: Do not set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` in prod — it is a leak vulnerability. List only known origins.

s5.title: Security: scopes, sandboxing, secrets
s5.why: An MCP server is RCE surface for an LLM. One careless tool with `exec()` and the model can wipe prod.
instructions: Token scoping: the token in env — verify minimum permissions upstream. Not a root key.
Sandboxing: if a tool runs code/shell — isolate (Docker, firejail, vm2). Never `child_process.exec` on raw params from the model.
Confirm flow for destructive: tools with DELETE/UPDATE — explicit confirmation in response ("call confirm_delete with the same id").
Per-tool rate limits: otherwise the model burns quota in a loop.
Audit log: every tool call into structured logs with timestamp, params, result summary, caller id.
Secrets: only via env, never in code. Use a secret manager (1Password / AWS SM / Vault) to inject.

Bad vs good example:
Bad:
```ts
{ name: "run_query", handler: (args) => db.query(args.sql) } // SQL injection via the model
```

Good:
```ts
{
  name: "search_users",
  inputSchema: { properties: { email: { type: "string", format: "email" } } },
  handler: (args) => db.query("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = $1", [args.email])
}
```
If the model spams a tool in a loop — either a bug in logic (tool returns "retry") or rate limit needed: add a circuit breaker, after N consecutive identical calls return error.
s5.validate: The security checklist (6 items above) is filled in, each done/skip with rationale.
s5.tip: Threat model: "what happens if the model tries to harm you?" Not paranoia — prompt injection through resources is real.

s6.title: Publish to registry
s6.why: Without publishing the server only lives on your machine. Registry = distribution + discovery + versioning.
instructions: Prepare README: what it does, which tools, env vars, install command, minimal example config for Claude Desktop.
Version with semver. 0.x while API breaks, 1.0 = public stable.
Publish to npm (TypeScript) or PyPI (Python) with prefix `mcp-server-` or scoped `@org/mcp-*`.
Submit a PR to `modelcontextprotocol/servers` (community) OR your internal registry.
Add CI: every PR runs `inspector` smoke test and schema validation.
Internal server? Host in a private registry (npm Enterprise, internal PyPI). Do not push to public — leaks inner workings.
s6.validate: The server installs via `npx @org/mcp-name`, the config connects to Claude Desktop, tools are visible.
s6.tip: Internal server? Host in a private registry (npm Enterprise, internal PyPI). Do not push to public — leaks inner workings.

claude-code-project.title: Production-grade project with Claude Code
claude-code-project.subtitle: CLAUDE.md, hooks, subagents, MCP — a big project that does not turn into chaos
claude-code-project.whatItIs:
[[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] out of the box is already powerful. But in a big project without setup it quickly becomes the "smart but unpredictable teammate": breaks style, goes the wrong direction, burns tokens on the same thing.

A production-grade setup turns Claude Code into a reliable contributor: knows your architecture, does not touch what is off-limits, specializes per task, sees your internal tools, gets verified on every commit.
claude-code-project.approach: In layers. First the CLAUDE.md hierarchy (context and rules), then slash commands (repeatable operations), then guard-rails (hooks + permission policy), subagents (specialization), MCP (integrations), and finally headless mode for CI. Each layer is verified separately.
outcomes: You build a CLAUDE.md hierarchy (root → area → package) without duplication
You author custom slash commands for repeatable team workflows
You configure [[node:cc-hooks|hooks]] (pre/post-tool-use) for lint, audit, secret scan
You deploy [[node:cc-subagents|subagents]] for specialization (reviewer, test-writer, debugger)
You wire MCP to the team's internal services
You set up a permission policy (allow/deny) with a safe default
You run Claude Code in headless mode in CI

applyIn.title: Monorepo with 10+ packages
applyIn.description: CLAUDE.md hierarchy + per-package overrides — Claude respects local rules.

applyIn.title: Code review automation
applyIn.description: Subagent + headless mode in CI — review comments on PRs without human-in-the-loop for routine.

applyIn.title: On-call incident helper
applyIn.description: MCP to logs/metrics + slash command `/incident` → fast triage.

pitfalls: One giant CLAUDE.md of 2000 lines — the model partially ignores it.
Hooks that do not return exit code 0 correctly — they block all tool calls.
Subagents for every micro-task — overhead exceeds the benefit.
Permission policy `allow all` in headless CI — sooner or later it bites.
Forgetting `.claude/settings.local.json` in .gitignore — you commit secrets.

exercises.question: Set up a 3-level CLAUDE.md hierarchy (root, area, package). Verify Claude sees the context at each level — ask a question inside the package and ask it to cite rules.
exercises.hint: Do not duplicate — children only delta from the parent.

exercises.question: Configure a pre-tool-use hook that blocks `git push --force` to main. Break it on purpose — Claude must get an error, explain it, suggest an alternative.
exercises.hint: Hook exit code 2 = block with a message for the model.

s1.title: CLAUDE.md hierarchy
s1.why: CLAUDE.md is persistent context. Without a hierarchy in a monorepo everything is in one file — the model drowns.
instructions: Root `/CLAUDE.md` — global rules: stack, conventions, what is forbidden.
Area-level `/apps/web/CLAUDE.md` — specifics of that area (front, back, infra).
Package-level `/packages/auth/CLAUDE.md` — only delta from parent (package specifics).
Rule: child does not repeat parent, only extends/refines.
Size: root ≤ 200 lines, children ≤ 100. If bigger — move to `/docs` and link.

Example. /CLAUDE.md (root): `# Stack: TypeScript, pnpm, Turborepo` / `# Conventions: ESM only, no default exports, vitest for tests` / `# Forbidden: any in TS, console.log in production, raw SQL in code (ORM only)`. /apps/web/CLAUDE.md: `# Web app specifics` / `# Routing: TanStack Router (file-based)` / `# State: Zustand for global, React Query for server` / `# Tests: vitest + Testing Library, NO enzyme`.
If Claude ignores some rules — file too long or rules conflicting; shorten, move rare ones to /docs.
s1.validate: The hierarchy is visible to Claude (ask an init-like question — you see it reads multiple CLAUDE.md files).
s1.tip: In CLAUDE.md write "rules", not "tutorials". Long explanations → /docs with a link.

s2.title: Custom slash commands
s2.why: If you repeat the same prompt 3+ times a week — it is a slash command. Saves typing and standardizes.
instructions: Commands live in `.claude/commands/<name>.md`.
Each = markdown with instructions + `$ARGUMENTS` placeholders.
Filename = command name (`.claude/commands/review-pr.md` → `/review-pr`).
At the top of the command — frontmatter with `description`, `allowed-tools`.
Commit to the repo — the command becomes shared for the team.

Example. `.claude/commands/release-notes.md` with frontmatter (`description: Generate release notes from commits since last tag`, `allowed-tools: Bash, Read`) and body: get commits since the last tag via `git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --oneline`, group by type (feat/fix/chore/docs), write a human-readable summary, output in CHANGELOG.md format, version: $ARGUMENTS. Call: `/release-notes v2.4.0`.
s2.validate: `/help` shows your command, the call works, arguments are substituted.
s2.tip: Personal commands — in `~/.claude/commands/`. Project — in the repo. Project matters more: shared workflows = consistency.

s3.title: Guard-rails: hooks and permission policy
s3.why: [[node:cc-hooks|Hooks]] are shell scripts that Claude Code runs before/after tool calls: every Bash, Write, Edit goes through your policy. A permission policy (allow/deny) decides ahead of time what is allowed without asking and what is forbidden always — otherwise you get either "approve all blindly" or "constantly interrupts".
instructions: Hooks and permissions config in `.claude/settings.json` (project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (user).
Hooks: `PreToolUse` can block a tool (exit code 2 = block + message for the model); `PostToolUse` for audit, notifications, does not block.
Matcher — regex on tool name: `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit|MultiEdit`. Hook reads JSON from stdin (tool params), writes JSON to stdout (response/error).

Example settings.json hooks: `PreToolUse` matcher `Bash` → command `.claude/hooks/guard-bash.sh`; `PostToolUse` matcher `Edit|Write` → command `.claude/hooks/secret-scan.sh`. The guard-bash.sh script reads stdin, extracts `.tool_input.command` via jq, and on match against `rm -rf|git push.*--force.*main|DROP TABLE` prints `{"decision": "block", "reason": "Destructive command blocked by policy"}` and exits 2, otherwise exits 0.
Permission policy: `permissions` section in settings.json. `allow` — list of patterns (tool + matcher) allowed without asking. `deny` — list FORBIDDEN always (overrides allow).
Principle: deny — destructive (rm, force push, drop), allow — frequent safe (read, lint, test). Everything else will be asked — those questions signal "add to allow or deny".

Example permissions: allow = [`Bash(npm test:*)`, `Bash(pnpm lint:*)`, `Bash(git status)`, `Bash(git diff:*)`, `Read(**)`, `Edit(src/**)`]; deny = [`Bash(rm -rf:*)`, `Bash(git push --force*)`, `Bash(curl:*sh)`, `Write(.env*)`].

If a hook is silently ignored — check chmod +x on the script and that the path in settings.json is project-root-relative or absolute. If a hook blocks everything — exit code 0 = pass, 2 = block, others = warning; check the exit code at the end of the script.
If Claude still asks on allowed — the matcher did not match: `Bash(npm test)` ≠ `Bash(npm test -- --watch)`; use `:*` for wildcards (`Bash(npm test:*)`).
s3.validate: Ask Claude to run a forbidden command (`git push --force`) — it gets a deny/error with your explanation. An allow command (e.g. `npm test`) — runs without asking.
s3.tip: Project settings (committed) = team policy. Personal (`settings.local.json`, in .gitignore) = your individual permissions.

s4.title: Subagents: specialization
s4.why: [[node:cc-subagents|Subagents]] = separate context with a narrow role (reviewer, test-writer, debugger). They keep the main chat clean and solve the task better due to a focused prompt.
instructions: A subagent lives in `.claude/agents/<name>.md` (project) or `~/.claude/agents/` (user).
Frontmatter: `name`, `description` (when to invoke), `tools` (whitelist), optional `model`.
Body — the subagent's system prompt: role, style, output format.
Claude Code decides when to call a subagent (from the description) — or you call `@<name>` explicitly.
One subagent = one narrow task. Not a "universal assistant".

Example. `.claude/agents/test-writer.md` with frontmatter (`name: test-writer`, `description: Write vitest unit tests for new/modified TypeScript functions`, `tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash`, `model: sonnet`) and body: "You write vitest unit tests. Rules: one *.test.ts file per module; AAA structure (Arrange/Act/Assert); mock via `vi.mock`, not hand-rolled factories; cover happy path, edge cases, error path; do not write integration tests — that is another agent."
If a subagent is not auto-invoked — description too generic or conflicts with another agent; make it concrete: "vitest unit tests for TypeScript modules".
s4.validate: Say "write tests for src/auth/token.ts" — the main chat delegates to test-writer, you see it in the log.
s4.tip: A subagent should not "think for you" — it should execute clearly bounded work. If the description is vague, the main chat will not invoke it.

s5.title: MCP to internal services
s5.why: Without [[node:mcp|MCP]] Claude Code only knows files and shell. With MCP — it sees your tracker, docs, DB, metrics.
instructions: Config — `.mcp.json` at the project root (project-scoped, goes to git) OR `~/.claude/mcp.json` (user).
For each MCP server: `command`, `args`, `env`. Secrets via `${ENV_VAR}`, do not hardcode.
Check token scopes — prefer read-only over admin.
After adding — `/mcp` in Claude Code → you see connection status and tool list.
If you have your own server (see "Advanced MCP") — publish internally and connect here.

Example. `.mcp.json` with `mcpServers`: `linear` (command `npx`, args `["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-linear"]`, env `{ "LINEAR_API_KEY": "${LINEAR_API_KEY}" }`) and `internal-traces` (command `npx`, args `["-y", "@acme/mcp-trace-storage"]`, env `{ "TRACE_API_KEY": "${TRACE_API_KEY}" }`). Secrets come from `.envrc` (direnv): `export LINEAR_API_KEY=$(op read "op://Eng/linear/api-key")` and `export TRACE_API_KEY=$(op read "op://Eng/traces/api-key")`.
If a server is connected but tools are empty — the server started but declared no capabilities; check server logs via `claude --mcp-debug` or call the server manually via Inspector.
s5.validate: `/mcp` shows all servers connected, tools visible.
s5.tip: Secrets — only via `${ENV_VAR}` from a secrets manager, never hardcode in `.mcp.json`. Keep token scopes read-only.

s6.title: Headless mode in CI
s6.why: Claude Code is not only interactive. `claude -p` (headless) is a full CLI for CI: code review on PRs, auto-fix lint, generate changelog.
instructions: Headless syntax: `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format json`.
Auth in CI: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env (via GitHub Secrets).
Permissions in CI: explicit `--permission-mode acceptEdits` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions` (only in sandbox CI runner!).
Output: stream JSON — parse in your action.
Time budget: max 5-10 min per run, otherwise CI becomes a bottleneck.

Example. `.github/workflows/claude-review.yml`: trigger `on: pull_request`, job `review` on `ubuntu-latest` with permissions `contents: read` and `pull-requests: write`. Steps: `actions/checkout@v4` with `fetch-depth: 0`, then `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` with `api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}`, `mode: review`, prompt "Review the diff against main. Focus: bugs/edge cases, missing error handling, test coverage gaps. Skip: style/formatting (handled by linters). Post inline comments." and `allowed-tools: "Read,Bash(git diff:*),Bash(pnpm test:*)"`.

If the action exceeds the timeout — reduce scope in prompt ("only diff, not the whole file"), shrink allowed-tools, set max-turns. Permission denied on Bash in CI — the CI sandbox is isolated, there `--permission-mode acceptEdits` is safe, but do NOT use it on a self-hosted runner in prod.
s6.validate: PR opens → action runs → you see inline comments from Claude within 5 minutes.
s6.tip: Cost control: in CI use model `sonnet` (not opus) for routine tasks + `--max-tokens` cap. Otherwise budget blows up.

outputs: CLAUDE.md hierarchy, shared slash commands, hooks, subagents
